h: Parties with closed doors: why no Mamdani rises in India
dek: In Scroll, Debasish Roy Chowdhury writes that India's opposition, so pleased at Trump's setback in America, forgets that its own parties have no room for new people and rebel voices.
ank: Not a single press conference under Modi
body: Liberals around the world breathed a sigh of relief at the blow Trump's party took in America's midterm elections, and in India the relief was double. A Congress spokesperson called Trump America's Modi and went on to predict the same fate here. Debasish Roy Chowdhury says this hope is premature, because the two democracies are built very differently.

Trump openly flouts the rules of governance, while Modi has a hundred-year-old Hindutva movement behind him; he appears to follow the rules while slowly changing the rules themselves. Trump faces questions from journalists, while in India the prime minister has not held a single press conference in twelve years. Trump lost after his first term and was punished two years into his second; Modi has lasted twelve years, and even after 2024 the BJP has won six states and one Union Territory.

The writer's real argument is about what happens inside parties. In America's open, scattered system, new people find their way in. The grassroots campaign Zohran Mamdani ran in last year's New York mayoral race, built around everyday prices, is what changed the Democrats' strategy. This was possible because groups like the Democratic Socialists of America work like a party within the party, and primaries run by the state take the power to choose candidates away from party bosses.

In India the picture is the reverse. Parties hold no internal elections, decisions come down from the top and family dynasties carry on. Liberals dream of an Indian Mamdani, but according to the writer such a rebel would never even get a ticket, because tickets are handed out by the party's owners. An opposition with no room for dissenting groups and new faces ends up as a hollow electoral brand.
nazar: In our view the lesson is simple: clapping for America's result will change nothing here. As long as tickets, from the Congress to the regional parties, are handed out at the will of one family or one leader, a small-town labour leader, a Dalit or Adivasi worker, or a woman who came up through a movement will never reach the top.
The opposition talks of saving democracy, but it first has to bring democracy into its own house.
sawal: Should Indian parties choose their candidates through primaries?
ref: Primary election
In America, a first-round vote to pick a party's candidate, in which the party's supporters vote. It curbs the arbitrary power of the leadership.
Democratic Socialists of America
A left-wing American organisation that does not form a separate party but pushes its own candidates from inside the Democratic Party.
photo_note: The County Election, polling day in an American town, 1846

h: The nation's auditor went missing from the meeting of those who demand accounts
dek: P. Sesh Kumar, a former Director General of Audit at the CAG, asks why the CAG stayed silent at the national conference of public accounts committees when the questions were about its own work.
body: On 3 and 4 November, the chairs of public accounts committees from across the country met in Thiruvananthapuram. Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, Parliament's Public Accounts Committee chair K.C. Venugopal and Kerala Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan spoke, but the voice of the Comptroller and Auditor General, the CAG, was nowhere to be heard. P. Sesh Kumar, who has served as Director General of Audit at the CAG, wrote on Audit Day that no record carries a speech or message from the CAG, and that according to his sources a Deputy CAG sat there in silence.

The absence jars because the questions at the conference were aimed straight at the CAG: delays in action on its reports, how audit subjects are chosen and what the method of scrutiny is. Satheesan questioned the loss estimate in the 2G case and the analysis of the Vizhinjam port. The writer believes the 2G figure of Rs 1,76,645 crore was not a real loss but an estimated calculation, and that the CAG should have explained this itself from the stage.

The situation is worrying. In 2021-22 and 2022-23, Union government departments accepted only 18-20 per cent of the CAG's recommendations; in the states it was 28 to 48 per cent. Thousands of action reports are stuck. The Union audit reports placed in Parliament each year fell from an average of 40 in 2014-18 to 22 in 2019-23, and the number of audit staff has also shrunk.

The writer also points out that the CAG's press page does not even mention this conference, though meetings with officials, academics and foreign counterparts are recorded there. His advice: the CAG should speak at such conferences, make public its method for working out estimated losses, set a time limit for placing reports, share data with state legislatures and carry out multi-year audits of major central schemes.
nazar: The CAG is the institution that asks the government to account for public money. If its reports shrink and it shies away from questions by elected representatives, a major means of catching irregularities in schemes like rations, MGNREGA (the rural jobs scheme) or roads grows weaker. In our view, the silence of a constitutional body is also a way of escaping accountability.
sawal: Why did audit reports fall from 40 to 22 in four years?
ref: Public Accounts Committee
A committee of Parliament and state legislatures that examines the CAG's audit reports and asks the government to explain its spending. Its chair usually comes from the opposition.
Action report (Action Taken Note)
A government department's written reply on what steps it took on an objection raised in an audit. When these are stuck, it shows the audit's effect has not reached the ground.
photo_note: Representative image: a page from an old account ledger

h: The historian and the Sangh: examining R.C. Majumdar's saffron ties
dek: In ThePrint, researcher Sufal Bepari draws on the old weekly Swastika to show how close the famous historian Ramesh Chandra Majumdar was to Hindutva in post-Independence Bengal, and where he stood apart from it.
body: Ramesh Chandra Majumdar is counted among the most famous Indian historians of the twentieth century, but little has been written about his ties to Hindutva politics in Bengal after Independence. Sufal Bepari, a political science researcher at Vidyasagar University in Medinipur, has pieced this story together from old issues of the Bengali Hindu nationalist weekly Swastika. His focus is not Majumdar's scholarship but his links with the Sangh Parivar (the family of organisations around the RSS).

Irfan Habib describes him as a member of the Hindu Mahasabha. The writer found no proof of formal RSS membership, but Majumdar was certainly a patron and sympathiser, and in 1960 he presided over the closing of the Sangh's winter camp in Bengal. In the 1951-52 Bengal assembly election he contested Tollygunge North on a Bharatiya Jana Sangh ticket and came fifth with 1,783 votes. In 1971, at an event marking Syama Prasad Mookerjee's death anniversary, he took aim at Nehru.

The association lasted a long time. In 1963 he was a founding member of the Vivekananda Birth Centenary Committee, in 1968 he presided over events of the Kanyakumari memorial campaign led by Eknath Ranade, and in October 1969 he inaugurated the ABVP's 17th all-India conference in Kolkata. In 1973, at Yogakshema, an organisation set up by Sangh workers, his speech on national unity, citing Al-Biruni, Partition and the violence in Assam, was full of the very ideas that have long been called communal.

Even so, the writer stresses one difference. Majumdar clearly leaned towards Hindu nationalism, but he wrote history grounded in sources. His views on beef, caste and ancient society, and Jadunath Sarkar's portrayal of Sambhaji, do not fit the invented stories of today's Hindutva.
nazar: Today, as Hindutva in Bengal searches for its roots and its heroes, Majumdar's name is very useful to it. In our view this article is a reminder that a scholar's politics and scholarship should be judged separately, and that those who wave history like a flag are stung most by the same source-based honesty on which Majumdar himself stood.
sawal: Why do Majumdar's views on beef sting today's Hindutva?
ref: Swastika
A Bengali weekly from Bengal that has published Hindu nationalist ideas and news of Sangh activities. The writer combed through its old issues.
Bharatiya Jana Sangh
A party founded in 1951 by Syama Prasad Mookerjee, linked to the Sangh. The Bharatiya Janata Party emerged from it in 1980.
photo_note: Representative image: the Asiatic Society building in Kolkata

h: A cornered Netanyahu's last move: buying time
dek: Akiva Eldar, a former Haaretz columnist, says that Netanyahu, having lost his majority, is busy not forming a government but stopping his rivals from forming one.
body: Israeli journalist Akiva Eldar, who has been writing about Benjamin Netanyahu for thirty years, says he has never seen Netanyahu so cornered. His bloc won 53 seats in the election, eight short of the 61 needed for a majority. Sixty-seven members of the Knesset have recommended Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and a former army chief, who has 42 days to form a government.

The writer says that for Netanyahu the chair is not just power but a protective shield. The corruption trial running since May 2020 is in its final stage. Eisenkot's bloc has already brought bills for an official inquiry into the 7 October attack and for a term limit on the prime minister. In office he can delay proceedings; out of it, he will be just a defendant.

So, according to Eldar, Netanyahu does not need to form his own government, only to hold up his rivals. The first move is a proposal for a 'national unity government' that includes Ben-Gvir, Smotrich and the Haredi parties but not the Arab parties, even though Arab citizens are about 21 per cent of the population. The second move is inflammatory language: in Parliament's first session he called Ra'am and the Joint List supporters of terror.

The third move is the most dangerous. According to reports, Netanyahu has pressed Trump for a new wave of strikes on Iran, and former prime minister Ehud Barak has already warned of a situation in which some provocation turns into war and the new government is stalled. If all else fails, a seventh election since 2019 is his last way out.

Eisenkot's problem is that he promised to keep his distance from Netanyahu, the Haredim and the Arabs, all three, and keeping all three promises is impossible. The Haredi parties are demanding exemption from military service, while the Arab parties are ready to give support from outside. The writer recalls 1995, when an inflamed atmosphere ended in the assassination of Yitzhak Rabin.
nazar: One thing is clear from this debate: a long war can also become a leader's personal political need. A new attack on Iran means oil prices, the safety of the lakhs of Indians working in the Gulf and the instability of the whole region, so who forms Israel's government is not distant news for us.

In our view the biggest lesson lies in the treatment of Arab citizens. A democracy that treats the representatives of a fifth of its population as untouchable in government will stay stuck in counting a majority. This game of keeping minorities out of political power should look familiar to us too.
sawal: Will Eisenkot be able to form a government in 42 days?
ref: Knesset
Israel's 120-member parliament. A majority of 61 seats is needed to form a government.
Haredi
The ultra-Orthodox Jewish community, whose parties demand exemption from military service for religious students.
photo_note: Representative image: the building of Israel's parliament, the Knesset, in Jerusalem

h: A rush to mine Phulbari's coal, at the cost of land and water
dek: Bangladesh's government wants a roadmap for an open-pit mine in three months; the writer says a new, independent impact assessment must come first.
body: Bangladesh's energy minister Iqbal Hasan Mahmud Tuku told an economic conference in Dhaka that the time has come to extract Phulbari's coal through an open-pit mine. He said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has asked for a roadmap in three months and that talks on bidding have begun. The writer, Jannatul Naym Pial, accepts that the arguments about electricity, the import bill and foreign exchange are not light ones, but says deciding on these alone would be dangerous.

Phulbari in Dinajpur has an estimated 572 million tonnes of coal, of which about 475 million tonnes can be extracted. The biggest question is water. To keep an open-pit mine dry, groundwater has to be pumped out continuously, and the project's own estimate put this at 400 to 800 million litres a day, for 36-38 years. The surrounding villages depend on this very water.

The displacement figures do not match either. The company spoke of resettling 40,000 people; in 2012 UN experts warned that 50,000 to 1,30,000 people would be uprooted and up to 2,20,000 affected; and now a government estimate puts it at 18-20 thousand. The writer asks what will happen to the landless.

History must also be remembered. On 26 August 2006, police opened fire on a protest against the mine; three people were killed and hundreds injured. Four days later the government reached an agreement with the protesting National Committee and put a stop to open-pit mining. This month, more than 300 local people also rallied in favour of mining, on condition of compensation and resettlement.

The writer also asks who will benefit. In 2005 the company offered Bangladesh a royalty of only 6 per cent, and GCM Resources, which took its place, is still hoping for approval. He demands a new, independent environmental and social assessment before bidding, public results, a comparison with gas and renewable energy, and that the villagers truly be heard.
nazar: This story feels like our own. In Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha too, villages, fields and forests have been uprooted for coal, while the royalties and profits went elsewhere. Phulbari's 2006 victory was a great example of a people's movement.
In our view a three-month roadmap is a rush. A decision that will change water and land for four decades needs a full accounting and village-level consent first.
sawal: Why are the figures for those displaced in Phulbari so different?
ref: Phulbari movement
A people's movement in 2006 against an open-pit coal mine in Phulbari, Dinajpur. After three deaths in police firing, the government agreed to cancel the project.
Open-pit mine
A way of extracting coal straight from the surface by stripping off the top layer of land, which affects a large area, farms and groundwater.
photo_note: Representative image: a coal mine in Dhanbad, Jharkhand

h: America is making Iraq pay the price of its fight with Iran
dek: Emil Avdaliani writes that US pressure to shut border crossings will strengthen in Iraq the very forces Washington wants to weaken.
body: America's war with Iran has heated up again, Iranian strikes are hitting Bahrain and talks are stalled. Meanwhile Iraq's foreign minister Fuad Hussein said the US Treasury has asked it to close all but two of the crossings on its border with Iran. Emil Avdaliani, a professor of international relations in Tbilisi, sees this as an open contradiction in American policy.

In his view, Washington on one hand wants to withdraw troops and build a deeper partnership with Iraq, and on the other wants to drag it into its front against Iran. In October an Iraqi bank was sanctioned, and before that militia commanders. According to reports, Trump also threatened that Iraqi groups would be attacked if they fought on Iran's side.

The writer says that because of geography, history and religious ties, Iran's influence in Iraq is not limited to the militias; it runs through ministries and institutions too. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi himself comes from the Shia Coordination Framework, factions of which are close to Tehran. American pressure will weaken the Iraqi leaders who want ties with Washington, and pro-Iran groups will exploit it by calling it an attack on sovereignty.

Iraq's economy is already taking the blows of war. About 90 per cent of government revenue comes from oil, and losses from the disruption in Hormuz are estimated at around 60 billion dollars. Annual trade with Iran is about 12 billion dollars, with roughly another 5 billion for the Kurdistan region separately, and Iraq depends on Iranian gas for electricity. Truckers, farmers, traders and border towns live off this.

The writer concludes that if Iranian influence is to be reduced, it will happen slowly, through investment, ties with Turkey and the Gulf, and projects like the 'Development Road', not by putting locks on the border. Coercion will destabilise Iraqi institutions, swell anti-American mobilisation and push Baghdad further from cooperation.
nazar: We have seen this pattern in the US sanctions on Iran's Chabahar port and on oil purchases too, when India had to accept Washington's terms instead of serving its own neighbourhood and needs. The bill for big powers' wars is often paid by the small countries in between and by ordinary people living on the border.
In our view Iraq's story is a reminder that sanctions hurt truck drivers, farmers and homes left without electricity more than they hurt governments.
sawal: How dependent is Iraq on Iranian gas for its electricity?
ref: Shia Coordination Framework
An alliance of Iraq's Shia parties and groups, many with close ties to Tehran. The current government was formed with its support.
Development Road
A proposed road and rail project linking the Gulf to Turkey through Iraq, still at an early stage.
photo_note: Representative image: the Iranian border centre across the Muntheria crossing in Diyala, 2009

h: The BJP's 'Gandhis' sidelined: which way will Varun go now?
dek: D.K. Singh says that pushing Maneka and Varun Gandhi aside was always certain in the Modi-Shah BJP, and that Varun now has only a handful of paths left.
body: Sonia Gandhi's book 'Belonging' has reopened an old rift in the Nehru-Gandhi family. The book remembers Sanjay Gandhi warmly, but its tone towards Maneka Gandhi is harsh. D.K. Singh points out that no one stepped up to defend Maneka, who was a Union minister from 2014 to 2019.

According to the writer, mother and son are now isolated in the BJP. Varun was denied a Lok Sabha ticket in 2024, was left off the Rajya Sabha list last month too, and neither of them is named in the Uttar Pradesh BJP's 712-member executive. Maneka was removed from the national executive in 2021. In 2013, at 33, Varun became the party's youngest national general secretary, but he lost the post as soon as Amit Shah became party president in 2014.

Singh also recalls the old calculation. Vajpayee and Advani had gone to jail during the Emergency, so Indira's 'persecuted' daughter-in-law seemed useful to the party. The Modi-Shah BJP attacks the Congress for dynasty and elitism, and keeping 'Gandhis' in its own house weakened that line. On top of that, both spoke their minds: Maneka called for an inquiry into the sexual harassment allegations against M.J. Akbar, and Varun stood with the farmers at Lakhimpur Kheri and backed a legal guarantee for MSP (minimum support price for crops).

In 2004 Varun became the first Nehru-Gandhi to attend the RSS's Vijayadashami rally in Nagpur, and in 2009 he faced a case for an inflammatory speech against Muslims, in which he was later acquitted. Now he has few paths. Joining the Congress is possible only on paper, since Rahul Gandhi is fighting a direct battle with the RSS. Akhilesh Yadav invited him into the SP in 2023. The third path is to strike out alone, as his mother once did. The writer feels there is a plan behind Varun's silence.
nazar: This is not the story of just one family. It is a sample of how little room for dissent is left in today's BJP: speaking up for farmers or asking for an inquiry into a party minister can cost you dearly, however big your name.

But we must not forget that Varun's politics has also had a phase of hate speech. Whatever his next step, the real question for the ordinary voter is not his dynastic identity but where he stands on farmers, jobs and communal harmony.
sawal: Why is Varun missing from the Uttar Pradesh BJP's 712-member executive?
ref: Belonging
Sonia Gandhi's memoir, which records her account of the Emergency and of relationships within the family.
1 Safdarjung Road
Indira Gandhi's official home in Delhi, from which Maneka moved out in 1982; it is now a memorial museum.
photo_note: Representative image: 1 Safdarjung Road, Delhi, now the Indira Gandhi Memorial Museum

h: If the SIR decisions were unanimous, where are the records?
dek: A petitioner told the Supreme Court that the Election Commission could not produce a single contemporaneous document of approval by all three commissioners.
body: Rakesh Kumar Singh, the petitioner challenging the conduct of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, has filed a fresh affidavit in the Supreme Court. He says the Election Commission has repeatedly claimed that decisions on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls were taken jointly by all three commissioners, yet not a single record from that time has been placed before the court.

The petition alleges that Gyanesh Kumar took several key decisions alone, whereas under Section 18 of the 2023 law the Commission has to decide collectively. In his rejoinder affidavit the petitioner has asked for the meeting agendas, minutes, file notings, proposals and electronic approvals to be produced. According to him, the Commission has itself admitted that officials took steps that later had to be corrected, that the online form was changed, and that appeals concerning lakhs of voters were filed without being brought before the Commission.

The most serious objection is to an extra declaration added to online Form 6, which asks the applicant for details of a parent's or grandparent's entry in old electoral rolls. According to the petition, without any change to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, this declaration became nearly mandatory for online applicants.

The petitioner argues that a later correction cannot validate earlier decisions, and that work delegated to officials cannot replace the Commission's collective authority. The Commission says the entire process was lawful. The case is before the bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant.
nazar: For the institution charged with protecting every vote, not having a paper trail of its own decisions is no small thing. If a drive that adds and deletes the names of crores of people ran without recorded approval, the first to suffer are the poor and migrant voters who have no papers from their grandparents.
sawal: On whose approval were grandparents' details added to Form 6?
ref: SIR

Special Intensive Revision: a fresh, door-to-door check of the electoral rolls.
This time the condition of 'mapping' to old records caused the most controversy.
Section 18, 2023 law

The 2023 law on the Chief Election Commissioner and other commissioners.
Under it, the Commission should work unanimously, and by majority when they disagree.
photo_note: Representative image: voters holding identity cards stand in a queue, Tripura 2008

h: Bilkis Bano: once again it was decided without hearing me
dek: After the life sentences of two convicts were suspended, Bilkis Bano said she will challenge the order.
body: Bilkis Bano, who survived gang rape and the murder of seven members of her family in the 2002 Gujarat riots, said in a statement on Monday that for the second time the Supreme Court has passed such an order without hearing her. She learned of it from the newspapers. She said she will fight the order.

On 28 October a bench of Justice M.M. Sundresh and Justice Prasanna B. Varale suspended the life sentences of two convicts and granted them bail. The court cited more than 17 years in jail and the severe disability of one convict. The order came on appeals against the Bombay High Court's 2017 verdict.

Bilkis wrote that she is afraid again, both for her children and of losing her faith in justice. In March 2002 she was 19 and five months pregnant when a mob attacked her family as they fled Randhikpur in Dahod district. Among those killed was her three-year-old daughter Saleha.

The two are among the 11 convicts whom the Gujarat government released in August 2022. In January 2024 the Supreme Court cancelled that release and sent them all back to jail. Bilkis says no woman should be forced to fight for justice her whole life.
nazar: Suspending a sentence without hearing the survivor may be legally defensible, but the basic principle of justice is that the person who was wronged is heard in court. Bilkis's 24-year fight shows that in our country, for a woman who survived rape and communal violence, even a verdict is not the final stop.
sawal: Why should hearing the survivor not be required before a sentence is suspended?
ref: Suspension of sentence

While an appeal is pending, a court can halt a convict's sentence and grant bail.
This does not end the conviction; the appeal is decided later.
The 2022 release

On 15 August 2022 the Gujarat government released all 11 convicts by granting them remission.
In January 2024 the Supreme Court said Gujarat never had this power at all.
photo_note: Representative image: the Supreme Court building in New Delhi

h: A Nanded firm beat Meta in BJP ad spending
dek: A Scroll investigation: behind C.N.X. Media, which got Rs 28.5 crore from the BJP in four state elections, is a 32-year-old consultant who now wants to be a Hindutva leader.
body: C.N.X. Media, a tiny firm run from a Pune suburb, earned almost twice as much from the BJP's election ads as Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram. According to the BJP's expenditure statement to the Election Commission, the firm received Rs 28.5 crore in the assembly elections in Bihar, West Bengal, Kerala and Assam, against Rs 15.2 crore for Meta.

The BJP declared total spending of Rs 530 crore in these elections, of which about Rs 174 crore went on media advertising. Google India came first with 26 per cent of this, and C.N.X. Media second with about 16 per cent. The firm registered with the tax department only in May 2025. Earlier reports had linked it to a company owned by a Delhi pollster, but Scroll found that company had shut down back in 2017.

Using GST records, Scroll traced it to 32-year-old Sarjerao Dhage of Umri in Nanded district. He admitted his firm ran the BJP's digital campaigns but declined to give details, citing confidentiality agreements. He describes his work as influencer marketing.

This year Dhage has returned to Umri and emerged as a Hindutva activist. Pamphlets he distributed during Navratri spoke of protection from 'love jihad' and of setting up a 'Hindu Legal Defence Force'. He says he is neither with the BJP nor against it, only with Hindutva.
nazar: This story shows that the real cost of elections has moved from posters and banners to phones, through influencers and unknown firms, where the accounts are murkiest. When campaign money and the politics of hate appear in the same hands, the Election Commission will have to look not just at the amounts but at the routes they take.
sawal: Whose phones did the Rs 28.5 crore campaign actually reach?
ref: Influencer marketing

Promoting a product or party through people with large followings on social media.
It has grown fast in elections, and its cost is often not clearly recorded.
photo_note: Representative image: a campaign poster from the first general election of 1951-52

h: Twenty years of the Forest Rights Act, and claims in Madhya Pradesh are still being rejected
dek: At a public hearing in Bhopal, Adivasis from 35 districts alleged evictions, burning of crops and interference by the forest department.
body: On 12 November, more than 500 Adivasi (indigenous) and forest-dependent people from 35 districts came to a public hearing held by the Lok Swashasan Abhiyan at Gandhi Bhavan in Bhopal. The five-member panel included former Supreme Court judge Justice A.K. Patnaik. People complained of homes demolished, crops burned, pesticides sprayed on their fields and false cases. Some said they were getting eviction notices even after receiving land titles.

According to government data cited by the organisation, out of 7.66 lakh individual claims only 2.6 lakh had received titles by June 2026. Less than 10 per cent of the potential area for community forest rights has been recognised. Of the claims re-examined on the Van Mitra portal launched in 2019, about half had been rejected again by January 2025.

Rajesh Kanoje of the Adivasi Mukti Sangathan in Barwani alleges that the forest department plants trees under CAMPA on titled land, puts up fences and influences gram sabhas (village assemblies). According to him, officials themselves do not follow the maps.

According to the organisation, 9,058 families were removed from 109 villages in seven tiger reserves, often without their rights being settled. The report does not include the state government's or the forest department's side.
nazar: If, in the state with the country's largest Adivasi population, more than half the claims are still stuck in files two decades on, this is a failure not of the law but of the will to implement it. Turning the right to the forest into a welfare scheme takes power away from the gram sabha.
sawal: Why were half the claims rejected again on the Van Mitra portal?
ref: Forest Rights Act, 2006

A law recognising the rights of Adivasis and traditional forest dwellers to forest land and resources.
Its Section 4(5) bars eviction until a claim is decided.
CAMPA

The compensatory afforestation fund, used for planting trees to make up for forests that are cut.
The allegation is that this planting is often done on land Adivasis farm.
photo_note: Representative image: a Baiga Adivasi mother and child

h: States and districts will pay fines if the Yamuna gets dirtier
dek: The Supreme Court said any state or district in which the Yamuna's water worsens as it passes through will be held accountable and penalised.
body: A bench of Justice Manoj Misra and Justice Manmohan has said that if the Yamuna's water worsens on any parameter between where it enters and where it leaves a state, Union Territory or district, that place will be held accountable and penalised. The Central Pollution Control Board has been asked to devise a formula for recovering damages from polluters and from officials found negligent in inspections.

The court mentioned 520 drains that pour dirty water into the Yamuna. It accepted that pollution has grown despite huge sums being spent, and that building new sewage treatment plants alone will not clean the river. Not one of Delhi's 37 plants met all the prescribed standards.
Discrepancies were also caught in Delhi's Yamuna action plan. The plan showed no encroachment on 35 water bodies in Zone 'O', while the government's own annexure recorded encroachment on all of them.

All treatment plants have been ordered to install tamper-proof smart meters within a month and put daily data online. The board will carry out surprise inspections every quarter, and each state will appoint a senior nodal officer within two weeks.
nazar: Money has been poured into cleaning the Yamuna for years, and the river is just as sick. The court's focus now is that the account of the filth be written at every border, so that no state can pass the blame to another. What remains to be seen is whether the poor to be removed from Zone 'O' are resettled with the same strictness.
sawal: Why does not one of Delhi's 37 plants meet the standards?
ref: Zone 'O'

The Yamuna floodplain and riverbank area in the Delhi Master Plan.
It is meant to be kept green, but there has been large-scale construction here.
Common but differentiated responsibility

A principle from climate negotiations that the court applied to the Yamuna.
Each state's responsibility will be set according to its pollution and its capacity.
photo_note: Representative image: a man picking waste in the Yamuna

h: Dalit researchers' fellowships stuck for five months
dek: JRFs under the National Fellowship for Scheduled Castes have not been paid for two months and SRFs for five months; MP Chandrashekhar Azad has written to the minister.
body: Money from the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment's National Fellowship for Scheduled Castes (NFSC) has not reached Dalit researchers across the country for months. According to the researchers, Junior Research Fellows have not been paid for the last two months and Senior Research Fellows for the last five.

The body that runs the scheme, the National Scheduled Castes Finance and Development Corporation, is reportedly saying that the allocated budget has run out. The researchers say that despite repeated queries they are given neither a clear reason nor a date. Expected payment dates have been pushed back several times.

MP and Bhim Army chief Chandrashekhar Azad has written to Social Justice Minister Dr Virendra Kumar, saying that selected researchers should not be punished for administrative negligence. According to him, managing rent, food and daily expenses for months without money has become hard, and research work is also stalling.

The letter makes five demands: release all dues at once, inquire into the reasons for the delay, provide the full budget on time, set up a transparent, time-bound payment system, and fix accountability on the officials responsible. The report records no response from the ministry.
nazar: For Dalit researchers a fellowship is not a reward but the support without which many are forced to give up their studies. When the government talks of participation in higher education and then holds back money for five months, the burden falls on the very homes that have no other support.
sawal: How is a researcher to pay rent after five months without a fellowship?
ref: NFSC

The central government fellowship for Scheduled Caste students doing M.Phil and PhD.
It pays at the JRF rate in the early years and at the SRF rate later.
photo_note: Representative image: the reading room of IIT Delhi's Central Library

h: AAMSU says Assam picked out Muslim homes for demolition
dek: The All Assam Minorities Students' Union said in Delhi that after the eviction drives, thousands of families are living under the open sky with no rehabilitation.
ask: Stop arbitrary evictions, rehabilitate the uprooted families
body: At a press conference in Delhi on Tuesday, the All Assam Minorities Students' Union (AAMSU) alleged that the Assam government's eviction drives are being carried out selectively against Muslim families. A 10-point charter of demands has also been submitted to the President.

The union's president, Mohammad Imtiaz Hussain, said they are not against clearing government land; their objection is to the arbitrary and discriminatory way it is being done. According to him, homes, mosques, madrasas and graveyards were demolished, but the uprooted families got no water, no toilets and no schools.

Hussain gave several examples. He alleged that in Luthumari in Lakhimpur, of 300 families holding certificates from 1974, 173 were removed and 127 were left alone, and all those removed were Muslims. In Uriamghat, described as the Rengma Reserve Forest, more than 30,000 people still live, he said. In Boginadi, he said, the homes of families resettled after the 1983 violence were also pulled down despite a High Court direction.

The union also raised questions about the Foreigners' Tribunals, D-voters and the proposed revision of the voter list, and said people removed from Hasila Beel in Goalpara are living in tents. No response from the government to these allegations is recorded in the report.
nazar: Eviction is not only a question of land, it is a question of equality. If in the same village one community's homes stand and another's fall, the rule of law grows weaker. Rehabilitating people uprooted by the Brahmaputra's erosion is a basic duty of any government.
sawal: Why were only these 173 families in Luthumari removed?
ref: D-voter
People marked 'doubtful' on Assam's voter list since 1997, whose citizenship is decided by Foreigners' Tribunals. They lose the right to vote.

h: Twelve climb a water tank in Bathinda over their right to land
dek: Seeking ownership of the plot they have lived on for three generations, a family accuses the sarpanch of getting the land registered in her own name.
ask: Give ownership of the plot settled for three generations
body: On Sunday morning in Dayalpura Mirza village in Bathinda district, 12 people, men, women and children, climbed a water tank. Their demand is ownership rights over the plot where their family has lived for three generations.

Among the protesters are Gurtej Singh and Amritpal Singh. They allege that the village sarpanch Surinder Kaur, her son Gursewak Singh and the panchayat secretary got the land recorded in their own names with the help of revenue department officials. The family says it built a house on this very land and has lived here for years.

From the tank they raised slogans against the sarpanch, her son, the panchayat secretary and the tehsildar. They said they had been running around for a long time to get the matter settled and had to take this step to draw attention.

A large police force reached the spot and kept trying to bring the people down safely. By evening most had come down, but three men stayed on the tank. According to the police, someone had donated this land years ago and the family later sold it, which has angered those occupying it. The SDM (sub-divisional magistrate) was trying to persuade them. The sarpanch's side is not in the report.
nazar: When a family has to climb a water tank with its children for the papers to its own roof, it raises questions about both village land records and the power of the panchayat. Such disputes should be fairly examined at the tehsil office desk, not on top of a water tank.
sawal: In whose name, and how, was the Dayalpura Mirza plot recorded?
ref: Intaqal (mutation)
The process of changing the owner's name in land revenue records. Most land disputes in villages begin with allegations of fraud in this step.

h: Anganwadi workers' sit-in in Kotdwar enters its seventh day
dek: The chief minister announced a rise in honorarium but did not say how much, so workers from four blocks are holding on to their protest.
ask: Raise honorarium by Rs 140 a day, give Rs 10 lakh on retirement
body: The sit-in by Anganwadi (village childcare centre) workers in Kotdwar, Pauri district, continued for the seventh straight day on Monday. Workers, helpers and mini-Anganwadi workers from the Dugadda, Jaiharikhal, Rikhnikhal and Nainidanda blocks are taking part.

The anger is because on 9 November the chief minister announced that the honorarium would go up from December, but did not say by how much. The workers say the sit-in will continue until the amount is made clear, and the state leadership has also asked them to keep the protest going.

They demand that the honorarium of Anganwadi workers be raised by Rs 140 a day, and that of helpers and mini-workers by Rs 70 a day. They also want a one-time payment of Rs 10 lakh from the contributory welfare fund on retirement.

The sit-in was led by district president Basanti Rawat and block president Sangeeta Bhatt. Through SDM Sandeep Kumar, the workers sent a memorandum to the forest minister raising the safety of workers in villages next to forests. They recalled Anjana Devi, an Anganwadi worker from Charekh, who was killed in a bear attack.
nazar: In the hills, the load of nutrition and vaccination in every village rests on these women's shoulders, yet the account of their earnings is left to announcements. Such a delay in naming the honorarium amount, and the neglect of their safety on forest paths, both show that this work is still kept cheap by calling it 'service'.
sawal: Why did the chief minister not say how much the honorarium will rise?
ref: Honorarium

Anganwadi workers get an honorarium, not a salary, which means they are not treated as government employees.
That is why rights like minimum wage and pension stay out of their reach.

h: Over 500 sanitation workers in Tambaram stop work and strike
dek: Amid a plan to hand four zones to a private company, workers of the fifth zone are refusing transfers to other places.
ask: No transfers, let us work where we are
body: More than 500 sanitation workers of the fifth zone of Tambaram Municipal Corporation, next to Chennai, have refused to come to work and gone on strike.

The root of the dispute is a new plan by the corporation. Tambaram corporation has five zones. Under the plan, sanitation work in four zones will be done by a private company, and only in the fifth zone will the corporation's own government staff work. According to the report, as part of this change the current workers of the fifth zone may be sent to other zones.
The workers' demand is simple: they should not be transferred to another zone and should be allowed to work where they are now.

The strike is expected to hit garbage collection, street cleaning and other essential services in the fifth zone. No statement from corporation officials is in the report, but it expressed hope that the administration will talk to the workers and find a solution. In recent months there has also been a long protest in Chennai against the privatisation of sanitation work in Tamil Nadu.
nazar: Every decision to give sanitation work to contractors first shakes those very workers, most of whom are Dalits and whose job security is already weak. The city's cleanliness depends on them, so changing their place and terms of work without asking them is not right.
sawal: Which company will get Tambaram's four zones?
ref: Privatisation of sanitation

Municipal corporations give garbage collection and cleaning work to private companies on contract.
Workers' unions say this cuts permanent jobs, wages and safety.

h: Leh hunger strike in its fifth day, Apex Body turns down invitation
dek: The Leh Apex Body and the KDA say there will be no talks until the December elections are put off; about 200 people are on hunger strike.
ask: Postpone the December elections, then hold formal talks
body: The hunger strike at NDS Park in Leh reached its fifth day on Monday. According to Chering Dorjay Lakruk, president of the Leh Apex Body (LAB), about 200 people are on fast, even though protests and fasts are banned under the model code of conduct.

The new turn is that Ladakh's organisations have rejected the Centre's offer of talks. The Home Ministry had signalled talks in the second week of December. Lakruk called it an informal invitation and said there would be no talks until the elections to the Hill Council (LAHDC) are postponed to June next year.

In December, panchayat, municipal and LAHDC elections are due together in eight new districts. The organisations fear that with hurried elections the Centre will start talking to elected representatives instead of them. Lakruk says holding elections in the harsh winter is wrong, because more than 25 per cent of the population moves out, and that they no longer trust the Centre.

Talks have been stalled since the meeting of 15 October. Since 2023 the LAB and the Kargil Democratic Alliance have been demanding a legislature and constitutional safeguards like Article 371. They also want the inquiry report into last September's Leh firing. Sonam Wangchuk was removed from the protest site on 11 November and placed under house arrest.
nazar: When even the invitation to talks is informal and elections are set in the depth of winter, the suspicion of Ladakh's people is understandable. The way to win back trust runs through formal talks and making the Leh firing report public, not through house arrest.
sawal: If 25 per cent of the people are away in winter, who are the elections for?
ref: Article 371

This article of the Constitution gives several states special provisions for land, culture and local laws.
Ladakh's organisations want similar protection.

h: Manipur shuts down over killing of four Naga civilians, clashes in Imphal
dek: A 24-hour bandh by the Native People's Committee brought life to a halt in the valley and the Naga hills; police fired tear gas in Chingmeirong.
ask: Punish the killers of the four civilians, protect native people
body: A 24-hour bandh (shutdown) called by the Native People's Committee, Manipur (NPCM) against the killing of four Tangkhul Naga civilians was observed across the state on Monday. It ran from Sunday midnight to Monday midnight and was called together with civil society groups from both the hills and the valley.

According to the report, normal life came to a near standstill in the valley and the Naga hill areas. In Imphal, shops at Singjamei market stayed fully shut, and at Khwakeithel market women gathered to enforce the bandh. The bandh was also felt at the district headquarters of Ukhrul, Kamjong and Chandel.

In Imphal's Chingmeirong, bandh supporters and police clashed. NPCM volunteers allege that police broke their megaphones, which started the confrontation. Security forces fired tear gas shells to disperse the crowd.

Hospitals, ambulances, fire services, water, electricity and the media were exempt. The NPCM has demanded immediate justice for those killed and appealed to the state and central governments to restore peace, protect native people and punish the attackers. No government response is recorded in the report.
nazar: After more than three years of violence, ordinary civilians in Manipur are still being killed in ambushes, and people are left with no way to respond except a bandh. This time groups from the valley and the hills stood together, which is news in itself. The government's silence on the demand for justice could break this trust.
sawal: How did broken megaphones in Chingmeirong spark a clash?
ref: Tangkhul Naga

A Naga tribe living in Manipur's Ukhrul and Kamjong districts.
It is rare for Naga groups of the hills and valley organisations to call a bandh together.

h: A father returns to Nangarhar, where only war's poison remains
dek: This Al Jazeera Witness film looks at the damage in Afghanistan that never enters the body count: the effect of decades of war on soil, water and health.
photo_note: A scene from the film
body: War reporting often stops at counting the dead and the displaced. This film, released on 17 November 2026 in Al Jazeera's Witness series, opens another account: the damage that stays in the land, the water and people's bodies even after the bombs stop. The film's title itself states its subject: Afghanistan's ruined villages and the environmental cost of decades of war.

At the centre of the story is Ibrahim, who now lives in Kabul and is a father. In the film he returns to his old home in Nangarhar province in eastern Afghanistan. The area borders Pakistan. According to the film's introduction, the village where he spent his childhood is now in ruins, and the families who have stayed on speak of health problems they link to pollution left behind by the war.

The film was made by Ibrahim Sulaiman Khel and Matty Furtado together, so the man behind the camera is also a character in the story. Ibrahim records the destruction, meets the families who remain and at the same time thinks about his own family: what life would have been like had they stayed, and whether his family can ever return to this home.

Knowing Nangarhar's background matters. From the Soviet invasion of 1979 to the withdrawal of American troops in 2021, this province was a battleground in nearly every phase of fighting. In April 2017 the United States dropped its largest non-nuclear bomb in Achin district of this very province; the stated target was tunnels of fighters linked to the Islamic State. Landmines, unexploded shells and ruined fields have become the mark of this region.

The environmental damage from war is the least counted damage anywhere in the world. Pollution from military activity is often not recorded in any official figure, and no one examines the villages whose water or soil has been spoiled. So people's complaints about where their illness came from rest mostly on their own understanding and experience, and the film too presents them as the families' own beliefs.

The film's strength is its personal view. It is not an expert's report but the journey of a father standing between his roots and his children's future. Going home here is not just a tender memory but a question: how safe is it to settle again on poisoned land?
nazar: Five years have passed since the war in Afghanistan ended, but its debris is still in the soil of its villages. The powers that fought this war took no responsibility for cleaning the land or for the health of its people. Even at climate summits, military pollution is often left out of the accounting.

For India this is not a distant story. Ruined villages, displaced families and degrading land in our neighbourhood are tied to the stability of the whole region. The real cost of war is paid by people who had nothing to do with it.
sawal: Whose duty is it to clean Nangarhar's poisoned land?
ref: Nangarhar

A province in eastern Afghanistan bordering Pakistan.
Its capital is Jalalabad; it has been a war zone for decades.
Witness
Al Jazeera English's documentary series of films by independent filmmakers from around the world, focused on ordinary people.

h: By making Bhagat Singh a god, we buried his questions
dek: Prabhat Praneet's review of Ashok Kumar Pandey's new book shows which parts were quietly left out when Bhagat Singh's image was built.
photo_note: A block-printing craftsman of Punjab, around 1875
body: When a hero becomes an idol, the times around him and his doubts disappear. Every generation fills him with what it likes. Prabhat Praneet's review starts from this point and reads Ashok Kumar Pandey's book Hinsa-Ahinsa aur Bhagat Singh (Violence, Non-violence and Bhagat Singh) through this lens. The book is published by Yuvaan Books.

The reviewer mentions two letters. One is from a nineteen-year-old Bhagat Singh, out on bail in the Dussehra bomb case, asking a friend to get books sent from America and for news of his exiled uncle Ajit Singh. The other was written to his younger brother Kulbir about twenty days before his hanging, in which a worried elder brother talks about earning a living and matters at home. According to the reviewer, this domestic face hardly appears in the popular image.

The review's big question is what was chosen from Bhagat Singh's writing and what was left out. Socialists, the Left, the Right and Khalistanis have all claimed him, and each had to ignore some part of his ideas.

The book lays out the background from 1857 to the years after the First World War, and shows the influence of Kartar Singh Sarabha and the shadow of the Irish and Soviet revolutions. It also deals at length with the break-up of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association, informers and mutual distrust.

On the relationship between Gandhi and Bhagat Singh, the book says the quarrel was over method, not enmity. For this the reviewer cites the 1929 telegram in which Bhagat Singh asked young people to give up bombs and pistols, and his statement that he was not a terrorist.
nazar: Bhagat Singh is on the poster at every stage today, but his books, his atheism and his socialism are rarely read. A poster asks no questions, so everyone finds it convenient.
In Deshkaal's view, such books matter because they give the hero back as a human being, and one can argue with a human being, not with a god.
sawal: Why do we so rarely hear Bhagat Singh's letter to Kulbir?
ref: Hindustan Socialist Republican Association
A revolutionary organisation formed in 1928, whose members included Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad and Sukhdev.
Kartar Singh Sarabha
A young revolutionary of the Ghadar Party, hanged in 1915; Bhagat Singh considered him his ideal.

h: Bulldozers on books in Bengal, and old memories of the pandals
dek: Baby Shaw writes that in Bengal, where people touch a book to their forehead if their foot brushes it, books were thrown into rubbish bins.
photo_note: Kalighat painting style of Calcutta, 19th century
body: In this instalment of her column C/O Bengal, Baby Shaw begins with a recent scene. According to the writer, a bulldozer knocked down bookshops in Bengal, and thousands of books, from science to literature, lay scattered on the road and were then dumped in municipal rubbish bins.

Against this she recalls the bond in Bengali homes where even an atheist touches a book to his forehead if his foot brushes it, and where on Saraswati Puja even a maths book is placed beside the goddess. At Durga Puja fairs, book stalls stood among the bangles, biryani and utensils, selling the Lakshmi Panchali (a household prayer book) as well as poetry from the Naxalbari years. From the sixties and seventies, Left stalls draped in red cloth introduced new readers to literature from around the world.

The piece also goes into history: the Bangla type made by Panchanan Karmakar in Hooghly in 1778, the first community puja at Guptipara in 1790, and the more than three thousand Sharadiya special issues (autumn festival annuals) published every year. The writer argues that books beside the pandal are a natural part of this tradition.

Then she recalls Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451, and the book burnings of Nazi Germany. On a remark by the Prime Minister and reports of Leftists being removed from educational institutions, she asks why every person who disagrees is branded.
Her conclusion is simple: a book can be criticised, but wiping it out ends the very room for debate.
nazar: Tearing down bookshops is a blow to a city's memory. Pavement and fair stalls were where a poor student could find a cheap book.
In Deshkaal's view, a system that begins to fear books also begins to fear its citizens' questions.
sawal: Whose books were these, thrown into the rubbish bins?
ref: Panchanan Karmakar
A blacksmith and craftsman of Hooghly who, in the 18th century, cast the first Bangla letters for printing.
Fahrenheit 451
Ray Bradbury's 1953 novel in which the state's firemen burn books.

h: Gorky's New York: real pain, one-sided gaze
dek: Reading Peele Daitya ka Nagar (City of the Yellow Devil), Praveen Pranav asks whether skyscrapers are only a sign of capitalism.
photo_note: Tanagra: The Builders, New York, 1918
body: Maxim Gorky reached New York in 1906. The city was then seen as the peak of industrial progress, but Gorky's wonder soon turned into fear and disgust. His account has now come out from Sambhavna Prakashan in Ashok Pandey's translation, titled Peele Daitya ka Nagar, and Praveen Pranav has written an interesting dissent on it.

The reviewer holds that every travelogue builds a third city: what was seen and what the traveller had assumed before setting out. Gorky went to America after the failed revolution of 1905 to raise funds and support, so his political gaze was fixed. The reviewer also recalls that American newspapers made an uproar over his unmarried companion and he had to leave his hotel.

But the reviewer does not call the portrayal of poverty false. Jacob Riis's 1890 book had already documented the crammed immigrant tenements and child labour. His complaint is that Gorky bends every scene towards one conclusion and does not ask why millions of people were being drawn there.

To make his point he goes as far as today's Shanghai and Shenzhen. The work of researchers like Pun Ngai and Jenny Chan on factories like Foxconn shows that exploitation happens even in a state that calls itself socialist, and Leslie Chang shows that for migrant women the same factory cities are also a path to earnings and freedom.
The review ends by saying that disagreeing with Gorky is fair, and good literature is the kind that leaves room for disagreement.
nazar: This review challenges the easy idea that exploitation is the mark of only one system. Migrant workers in India's industrial areas too arrive carrying both compulsion and hope.
In Deshkaal's view, to see a worker's suffering truly one must hear the worker's own voice, not a writer's ready-made conclusion.
sawal: Why did Gorky not see the hopes of New York's immigrants?
ref: Peele Daitya ka Nagar
Gorky's 1906 account of New York; for him the 'yellow devil' is a metaphor for gold and the dollar.
Jacob Riis
A Danish-American journalist whose 1890 book exposed the conditions of New York's slums.

h: Kadhi in the khejri's shade, and the woman who sweeps the lane
dek: Five poems by farmer-poet Nihal Singh look at fields, scarecrows and the labour that usually escapes notice.
photo_note: Village group, 1938
body: Nihal Singh is a farmer by profession and has been writing since 2005. According to Sammukh, his poems have appeared in magazines and web magazines such as Pahli Bar, Anunad, Setu and Kritya. His five poems on Sammukh read as if written not by a city poet but through the eyes of a man standing in a field.

The first poem is a memory of the wheat harvest. Father and siblings are in the field, mother brings a plain gram-flour kadhi (a yoghurt curry) at noon, and everyone sits under the khejri tree to eat. The poem sets down hunger, tiredness and family closeness without ornament.

The scarecrow poem has that figure of straw and old clothes that looks like a man and guards the crop. Squirrels and nilgai (blue bulls) are fooled by it, and the poem shows how much farming rests on watchfulness and making do. Another poem is steeped in memories of the mother's home, amid monsoon swings, dancing peacocks and Holi songs.

The sharpest poem is about the mehtarani, the woman who cleans the lane. On the day she does not come, the lane fills with filth, and only then is her worth understood. The last poem is a plain list of wishes: that women and men be equal, that dowry end, that officials be honest.
The language is everyday speech, the images are from the village, and the concern is society. To read these poems, visit Sammukh.
nazar: In Hindi poetry the village often comes as memory or romance. In Nihal Singh's poems the village is a place of work, where the face of the one who labours can be seen.
In Deshkaal's view, the poem on the mehtarani is a reminder of a truth our society looks away from: the one who cleans is the one least counted.
sawal: Why does the scarecrow, though it looks human, stand alone in the field?
ref: Khejri
A tree of the dry regions of Rajasthan and Haryana whose shade, leaves and pods are part of rural life.
Bijuka (scarecrow)
A man-like figure set up in a field to scare away animals and birds.

h: Ten poems by Rupam Mishra: love, the village and an answer to attacks
dek: Rupam Mishra's new poems on Sammukh range from the tenderness of love to village politics and trolling.
photo_note: Village girl, around 1937
body: Rupam Mishra's poem Ek Aitihasik Ladai Chhed Di Gayi Hai (A Historic Battle Has Been Started) was widely discussed recently. According to Sammukh's introduction, she faced attacks over it, and afterwards wrote two more poems with the same title. Both are in this new set, which has ten poems in all.

These two poems question those who mock a village woman's education, her language and her way of speaking, and take a jibe at so-called progressive debates that themselves see women through hierarchies of caste and status and film formulas.

The set opens with love. In one poem love feels like a weight, in which the speaker loses and finds her face in her lover's face. In another, someone's care slows her down and returns her to the softness of childhood. The poem about the gular flower speaks of a broken relationship, anger and the moral judgments passed on women, drawing on folk memory.

The poem titled Bombay Mein Love Jihad (Love Jihad in Bombay) is about village whispers, communal politics and the hypocrisy of men who forward a woman's private videos. Mere Paas Kagaz Nahin Tha (I Had No Papers) is about unemployment and a world of papers where a woman without a degree has her voice suppressed.
The last poem speaks of longing through images of desert and thirst. To read the poems in full, visit Sammukh.
nazar: Rupam Mishra brings the voice of a woman from an Awadhi village to the centre of Hindi poetry, and that is what bothers many people. The attack on her language is really an attack on that voice's right to be heard.
In Deshkaal's view, a poet's answer is her next poem, and these poems are that answer.
sawal: Who are the people who laugh at a village woman's speech?
ref: Gular flower
In folk belief the flower of the gular (cluster fig) is never seen, so it is an idiom for something rare or impossible.
Love jihad
A political slogan that paints interfaith love and marriage as a conspiracy, used in communal propaganda.

h: From dying languages to dead stars: poems by Harshit Mishra
dek: Harshit Mishra's poems place love among vanishing words, corrupt newspapers and melting glaciers.
photo_note: A Ranchi landscape and the evening star
body: Harshit Mishra is a young poet and this is his first appearance on Sammukh. According to the magazine's introduction, he explores his own experience and today's questions through poetry. In this set of nine poems two things keep returning: images of the cosmos and concern for things being lost.

The first poem is about languages and words that are dying. Its images are vanishing seasons, eroding inscriptions and drowning scripts, and its question is how a single letter survives amid all these extinctions.

The poem titled Panchvan Stambh (The Fifth Pillar) confronts politics most directly. Here poetry is seen as a force of democracy that stands against old tales of valour, royal courts and a sold-out press. Images like termites and weapons show what is being hollowed out from within.

The other poems speak of love and separation in the language of astronomy: black holes, the event horizon, drifting satellites and the light of dead stars that still reaches us. In Prem ki Paristhitiki (The Ecology of Love), melting glaciers, felled forests and dirty rivers become metaphors for the absence of love. The last poem is about loves the poet himself was not part of, that is, about trying to make others' experience his own.
To read the poems in full, visit Sammukh.
nazar: Poets of the new generation are bringing the language of science and climate into poetry, which is good news for Hindi. What matters is that these images become questions, not decoration.
In Deshkaal's view, the Fifth Pillar poem is the heartbeat of this set: when newspapers bow, the burden on poetry grows.
sawal: In an age of a sold-out press, whose side should poetry stand on?
ref: Event horizon
The boundary around a black hole beyond which even light cannot return.
Fifth pillar
A metaphor for a fifth watchdog force after democracy's three pillars and the press (the fourth pillar).
